children.translated_text: 1. The Province of <s>Kaśmīra</s> (Kashmir)

children.text:
oṃ śrī gaṇeśāya namaḥ |
	paṇḍitakalhaṇakṛtarājataraṅgiṇyāṃ prathame taraṅge ślokasaṃ 27 kaśmīrā |
	asyāḥ satīsara iti dvitīyaṃ nāma |
	asya niruktiḥ |
	kaṃ jalaṃ śmīrati calaty asmād iti śmīra smīra calane iti dhātor auṇādikaṃ rūpam |
	tathā ca nīlamate
children.translated_text: <s>Oṃ</s>, salutations to the glorious <s>Gaṇeśa</s>. In the <s>Rājataraṅgiṇī</s> composed by the <s>paṇḍita</s> <s>Kalhaṇa</s>, in the first <s>taraṅga</s> (wave), verse number 27: <s>Kaśmīrā</s>. Its second name is <s>Satīsara</s>. Its etymology: '<s>ka</s>' means water; '<s>śmīra</s>' — it moves from this [place] — from the root '<s>smīra</s>,' meaning 'to move,' it is an <s>auṇādika</s> form. And thus in the <s>Nīlamata</s> [Purāṇa]:

children.text: kaṃ vāri halinā yasmād deśād asmād apākṛtam |
children.translated_text: Since water (<s>ka</s>, <s>vāri</s>) was removed from this land by <s>Hali</s> (the ploughman, i.e., <s>Balarāma</s>),

children.text:
ataḥ sarvajagatkhyātaṃ kaśmīrākhyaṃ bhaviṣyati |
	anyac ca calanaṃ sampādanam ity api tanmatenaivāvagamyate |
	tathā ca kaśyapena sampāditasyāpi maṇḍalasya kaśmīrā iti nāma |
	etad api nīlamatād evāvabudhyate |
	tathā hi
children.translated_text: therefore it shall become known throughout the world by the name '<s>Kaśmīra</s>.' Furthermore, 'movement' also means 'bringing about' — this too is understood from the same view. And thus the province that was brought into being by <s>Kaśyapa</s> also [bears] the name <s>Kaśmīra</s>. This too is understood from the <s>Nīlamata</s> [Purāṇa] itself. For thus:

children.text: kaḥ prajāpatir uddiṣṭaḥ kaśyapaś ca prajāpatiḥ |
children.translated_text: '<s>Ka</s>' designates <s>Prajāpati</s>, and <s>Kaśyapa</s> is <s>Prajāpati</s>;

children.text: atas tadākhyayā tīrthaṃ kāśmīrākhyaṃ bhaviṣyati || iti |
children.translated_text: therefore, by his name, the holy land (<s>tīrtha</s>) shall become known as '<s>Kāśmīra</s>.'

children.text:
asya kaśmīrāpadasya kaśīra iti kāśmīrikabhāṣāyāṃ nāma vartate |
	ata eva kaśmīrotpannasya puṃsaḥ kaśur iti nāmāsti |
	punaś cānyamatena kaśmīrāpadaniruktau bahavo vibhedāḥ santi |
	tathā ca pārisekānuvādavidaḥ kecana kaśyapamar iti kathayanti |
	tanmatena kaśmīrabhāṣāyāṃ marpadasya gṛham ity arthaḥ |
	tathā ca kaśyapasya gṛham iti yāvat |
	anye tu kaśūr iti kaścid rākṣasaḥ pūrvasmin kāle babhūva |
	tasyaiva rakṣasasya marpadavācyā ekā apsarāḥ parīpadavācyā taddhastagatāpy āsīt |
	tābhyām eva sarvatra bambhramyamāṇābhyāṃ yad atra manohare maṇḍale svanivāsārthaṃ sthitir āsāditā |
	ataḥ kaśmar iti tadākhyayaiva prathām āgatyāyaṃ deśaḥ sarvajagatprasiddhaḥ sampanna ityādi svapustakeṣu likhanti |
	paraṃ tu asmin nāmani grāmīṇānāṃ nāgarikānāṃ ca kvāpy uccāraṇādiviṣaye bhedo nāstīti śam ||
children.translated_text: The word '<s>Kaśmīra</s>' has the form '<s>Kaśīra</s>' in the Kashmiri language. Hence, a man born in <s>Kaśmīra</s> is called '<s>Kaśur</s>.' Furthermore, according to another view, there are many variants in the etymology of the word '<s>Kaśmīra</s>.' Thus certain scholars of Persian translation say '<s>Kaśyapamar</s>.' According to that view, the word '<s>mar</s>' means 'house' in the Kashmiri language. And thus it means 'the house of <s>Kaśyapa</s>.' Others say that '<s>Kaśūr</s>' was a certain <s>rākṣasa</s> (demon) who existed in ancient times. That <s>rākṣasa</s> had an <s>apsaras</s> (celestial nymph) designated by the word '<s>mar</s>' (wife), who was also in his hands, designated by the word '<s>parī</s>' (fairy). Wandering everywhere, they settled in this beautiful province for their own residence. Therefore, by the name '<s>Kaśmar</s>,' this land became renowned throughout the world — thus they write in their own books. However, regarding the pronunciation of this name, there is no difference between villagers and city-dwellers anywhere. Peace.
2. <s>Nīlanāga</s> or <s>Varanāga</s>

children.text:
ślo 28 nambara 2 nāgādhīśena nīlena |
	ayaṃ nīlābhidho nāgaḥ kaśyaparṣiputraḥ |
	kaśmīrasthāne ka nāgānām adhipatiḥ |
	tena kaśyapena svakīyapitrā kaśmīrāsampādanakāla eva teṣām asaṃkhyānāṃ nāgānām ādhipatye sukarmaśikṣāyai kukarmaṇo nivṛttaye cābhiṣiktaḥ |
	śāhūbād puragaṇo yo 'dhunā śrīraṇavīrasiṃghapurā iti nāma dhārayati tasminn eva puragaṇe pīr pañcāl iti khyāto yo 'yaṃ kaśmīradeśasya pañcanadadeśasya ca madhye sīmaiva gaṇanīyatām āgataḥ parvato 'sti |
	tasmād eva parvatād ardhakrośamite kaśmīraunmukhyabhājimārge mahān aṣṭakoṇo 'gādhaḥ śītalajalaś ca nīlanāganivāsasthānaṃ jalāśayo vartate |
	asya varanāgaḥ nīlanāgaḥ vīranāgaḥ ityādīni nāmāni santi |
	tatra varanāgaḥ uttamanāgaḥ nīlanāgaḥ nīlanāmānāgaḥ nīlavarṇajalavān nāgaś ca vīranāgaḥ vīraś cāsau nāga iti grāmīṇas tu asya sthānasya vernāga iti nāma kathayanti |
	eto vernāg evādhunā grāmanāmāpy asti |
	varanāgaveranāgayoś ca sādṛśyam evoccāraṇe 'pi vartate |
	kecana bhṛṅgīśasaṃhitāmatāmatāśrayiṇo vīrī iti grāmasya nāmoktā vīrīviṣayasthito nāgaḥ vīrīnāga iti nāma kathayanti |
	asmiñ jalāśaye matsyā asaṃkhyāḥ santi |
	punaś ca asya jalāśayasya pāścāttye taṭa ekā bṛhacchālā purātanakālīnena jyahāṃgīrarājñā sampāditā yasyām ādhunikarājñā jīrṇoddhārādikaṃ niramīyata |
	atraika ārāmo 'pi purātanarājasampādito bhavati ||
children.translated_text: Verse 28, number 2: 'By <s>Nīla</s>, the lord of the <s>nāgas</s> (serpent-deities).' This <s>nāga</s> named <s>Nīla</s> is the son of the sage <s>Kaśyapa</s>. He is the chief of the <s>nāgas</s> at the site of <s>Kaśmīra</s>. At the very time of the creation of <s>Kaśmīra</s>, he was consecrated by his father <s>Kaśyapa</s> to the lordship of those innumerable <s>nāgas</s>, for training in good conduct and for turning away from evil deeds. In the township that is now known as <s>Śrīraṇavīrasiṃghapura</s> (Shahabad), at the place called <s>Pīr Pañcāl</s>, which is considered the border between the land of <s>Kaśmīra</s> and the land of the Five Rivers (<s>Pañcanada</s>, Punjab), there is a mountain. At a distance of half a <s>krośa</s> from that very mountain, on the road facing toward <s>Kaśmīra</s>, there is a great octagonal, deep, and cold-watered lake, which is the dwelling place of <s>Nīlanāga</s>. Its names are <s>Varanāga</s>, <s>Nīlanāga</s>, <s>Vīranāga</s>, and others. Among these: <s>Varanāga</s> means 'the excellent <s>nāga</s>'; <s>Nīlanāga</s> means 'the <s>nāga</s> named <s>Nīla</s>' or 'the <s>nāga</s> with blue-colored water'; <s>Vīranāga</s> means 'the heroic <s>nāga</s>.' Villagers call this place '<s>Vernāga</s>' (Verinag). And <s>Vernāga</s> is also the village name today. There is indeed a similarity in the pronunciation of '<s>Varanāga</s>' and '<s>Veranāga</s>.' Certain followers of the <s>Bhṛṅgīśasaṃhitā</s> tradition say the village name is '<s>Vīrī</s>' — the <s>nāga</s> situated in the <s>Vīrī</s> region is called '<s>Vīrīnāga</s>.' In this lake, there are innumerable fish. Furthermore, on the western bank of this lake, there is a great hall built by the ancient king <s>Jahāṅgīra</s>, in which renovation and restoration was carried out by modern rulers. Here there is also a garden established by the ancient king.
3. <s>Kapaṭeśvara</s>

children.text:
ślo 32 nambara 3 kāṣṭharūpam umāpatim |
	kāṣṭharūpaṃ kāṣṭhākṛtim umāyāḥ pārvatyāḥ patir bhartā śivaḥ |
	taṃ śivaṃ samyak sparśaṃ kurvatāṃ puruṣāṇāṃ bhogaprāptir bhavati |
	purā sarvair munibhiḥ prārthitena śivena teṣām evānugrahārthaṃ kapaṭenaiva svamūrtiprākaṭyakaraṇaṃ munibhyo 'ṅgīkṛtam |
	athaitādṛśaṃ śivād varaṃ labdhvāgatya cāsmin sthāne kāṣṭhā eva jale vivartamānā dṛṣṭāḥ |
	ato 'sya tīrthībhūtasya jalāśayasya kapaṭeśvara iti nāma kṛtam |
	adhunāpy asmiñ jalāśaya eko bṛhatkāṣṭho darīdṛśyate |
	nīlamate 'pi kapaṭeśvaramāhātmyavarṇane kapaṭena darśanaṃ dāsyāmi bhavadbhya iti munīn prati śivenoktaṃ yadā tadaivāgatya munibhir asmiñ jale kāṣṭhākṛteḥ śivasya darśanaṃ kṛtam |
	ato 'sya sthānasya kapaṭeśvara iti nāma sampannam |
	etādṛśy eva kathā vistare soktāsti |
	grāmīṇāḥ kaśmīrabhāṣayā asya sthānasya koṭyher iti nāma vadanti |
	ata eva kuṭahārapuragaṇo 'pi anenaiva nāmnā prakhyātiṃ prāptaḥ yasminn ayam eko grāmaḥ koṭyher iti nāmnādhunāpi kathyamāno 'sti |
	ayaṃ puragaṇaḥ pūrvoktāt śāhūbādapuragaṇād adhastāt krośacatuṣṭayena bhavati |
	asminn eva achyabal iti sthānaṃ sarvajanamate priyaṃ sarvataḥ prakhyātaṃ ca bhavati |
	grāmīṇā asya jalāśayasya saṅkarṣaṇ nāg iti nāmāpi vadanto vartante ||
children.translated_text: Verse 32, number 3: '[One should visit] the wooden form of the Lord of <s>Umā</s>.' The wooden form means having the appearance of wood; the Lord, the husband of <s>Umā</s>, i.e. <s>Pārvatī</s>, is <s>Śiva</s>. Those persons who properly touch that <s>Śiva</s> obtain enjoyment (material fulfillment). In ancient times, when all the sages had prayed to <s>Śiva</s>, he agreed, merely through deception, to manifest his own form for the purpose of granting them grace. Then, having obtained such a boon from <s>Śiva</s> and having come [to this place], in this very site, wood was seen revolving in the water. Hence the name <s>Kapaṭeśvara</s> ('Lord of Deception') was given to this sacred water-body. Even today, one large piece of wood is visible in a cavity in this water-body. In the <s>Nīlamata</s> [Purāṇa] too, in the description of the greatness of <s>Kapaṭeśvara</s>, when <s>Śiva</s> said to the sages, 'I shall grant you a vision through deception,' then indeed the sages came and beheld the vision of <s>Śiva</s> in the form of wood in this water. Hence this place came to be named <s>Kapaṭeśvara</s>. Such indeed is the story narrated in detail. The local people call this place 'Koṭyher' in the Kashmiri language. For this very reason, the <s>Kuṭahāra</s> district too has become famous by this very name, in which this one village is still called 'Koṭyher' even now. This district is four <s>krośas</s> (approximately eight miles) below the previously mentioned <s>Śāhūbāda</s> district. In this very [district] there is a place called 'Achyabal,' which is dear to all people and famous everywhere. The local people also call this water-body '<s>Saṅkarṣaṇa Nāg</s>.'
4. <s>Pāpasūdana Tīrtha</s> (The Pilgrimage Site that Destroys Sin)

children.text:
ślo 32 nambara 4 pāpasūdanaṃ tīrthāntaḥ |
	pāpāni sūdayati nāśayati yat tat pāpasūdanaṃ pāpanāśakaṃ tīrtham |
	tasmiṃs tīrthasaṃspṛśatāṃ snānaṃ kurvatāṃ puruṣāṇāṃ muktiprāptir bhavati |
	atrāpi mahāñ jalāśayo vartate |
	kaśmīrabhāṣāyām apy asya jalāśayasya pāpaharaṇ nāg iti nāma sarvatra grāmīṇāḥ kathayanti |
	ayaṃ jalāśayaḥ pūrvoktāt kuṭahārapargaṇād alpāntaravartini vāmapārśvapuragaṇe ādhunike kāle khourpor iti khyāta puragaṇe 'sti |
	tatrāpi sālīpāṃjamul iti khyātaṃ grāmadvayam asti |
	tayor eva madhye 'yaṃ pāpaharaṇ nāg ityabhidho jalāśayo vartate |
	atra pāpasūdanapāpaharaṇapadayoḥ sadṛśārthatvena saṃskṛte kaśmīrabhāṣāyām api asmin pade tādṛśo bhedo nāsti |
	ayaṃ jalāśayaś catuṣkoṇo nīlanāgād alpataro 'pi vartate |
	kadācana vāriparṇīyasya kaśmīrabhāṣāyāṃ muṅgol nāmāsti |
	tathācchādito 'pi dṛśyate ||
children.translated_text: Verse 32, number 4: '[One should visit] the <s>Pāpasūdana</s> (sin-destroying) pilgrimage site.' <s>Pāpasūdana</s> means that which destroys sins, the sin-removing <s>tīrtha</s> (sacred site). Those persons who touch that <s>tīrtha</s> and bathe [in it] attain liberation (<s>mukti</s>). Here too there is a great water-body. In the Kashmiri language too, the local people everywhere call this water-body 'Pāpaharaṇ Nāg' (the serpent lake that removes sin). This water-body is in the district on the left side, at a short distance from the previously mentioned <s>Kuṭahāra</s> district, in what is known in modern times as the 'Khourpor' district. There too, there is a pair of villages known as 'Sālīpāṃjamul.' Between those very two [villages] lies this water-body called 'Pāpaharaṇ Nāg.' Here, since the words <s>pāpasūdana</s> and <s>pāpaharaṇa</s> have similar meanings, there is no such difference in this term between Sanskrit and the Kashmiri language. This water-body is rectangular and smaller than <s>Nīlanāga</s>. At some time it is also seen covered with water-plants, called 'Muṅgol' in the Kashmiri language.
5. <s>Trisandhyā Devī</s> (The Goddess of the Three Junctures)

children.text:
ślo 33 nambara 5 sandhyā devī |
	samyak dhyāyate dvijātibhir yā sā sandhyā |
	sā cāsau devī dyotanaśīlā krīḍanaśīlā ceti asya tīrthavarasya sarvajagatprasiddhaṃ trisandhyā iti nāma sarve kathayanti |
	etat tīrthaṃ parvatasya kukṣau vartate |
	atra jalāśayo vartulākāro 'dhastāt saṃkucita uparitane bhāge vistṛtākāro bhavati |
	punaś cāyaṃ sadaiva śuṣko vasantakāle paripūrṇajalo grīṣmakāle trivāraṃ dine trivāraṃ rātrau ca paripūrṇajalaḥ śuṣkajalo 'pi bhavati |
	arthāt cañcalatayā jalavān jalābhāvavāṃś ca bhavati |
	tathā coktaṃ bhṛṅgīśasaṃhitādiśāstrabhedeṣu
children.translated_text: Verse 33, number 5: '<s>Sandhyā Devī</s> (the Twilight Goddess).' She whom the twice-born (<s>dvijāti</s>) properly meditate upon is <s>Sandhyā</s>. She is indeed the goddess — shining and playful in nature. Everyone calls this most excellent <s>tīrtha</s> by its universally famous name '<s>Trisandhyā</s>' (the Three Twilights). This sacred site is situated in the hollow of a mountain. Here the water-body is circular in shape, contracted at the bottom and expanded in form at the upper part. Furthermore, it is always dry [in winter], full of water in the spring season, and in the summer season it becomes full of water and dry three times during the day and three times during the night — that is, due to its fluctuating nature, it is sometimes with water and sometimes without water. And thus it is stated in the <s>Bhṛṅgīśa Saṃhitā</s> and other variant <s>śāstras</s> (treatises):

children.text: sadā śuṣkā madhau pūrṇā grīṣme cañcalavāhinī |
children.translated_text: Always dry in the spring, full in [late spring], with fluctuating flow in the summer,
flowing at three times [of the day], she is <s>Sandhyā</s> — that <s>Sandhyā</s> is the giver of liberation (<s>mokṣa</s>).

children.text:
ato grīṣmakāle jyaiṣṭhe māsi yathā prabhāte madhyāhne sāyaṃkāle ca sandhyopāsanaṃ kriyate |
	tathaivāsya tīrthavarasya yātrā sandhyeva bhavati |
	ayaṃ jalāśayo madhye pārśvayoś ca vartulākāraiḥ prastarair bharito 'sti |
	yasmin kāle sandhyāṃ vidhāya jalaṃ śuṣkatāṃ gacchati tasmin kāle tebhya eva pāṣāṇarandhrebhya ākhavo nirgatya bhaktaiḥ pūjārthaṃ jalāśaye pātitam akṣatādikaṃ bhakṣayanti |
	asya tīrthavarasya samīpe saptarṣīṇāṃ saptajalāśayā bhavanti |
	tebhya ekā kulyāpi nirgacchati |
	sālpā nady asya parvatasthatīrthavarasyādhastād vartate |
	sandhyākaraṇavelāyāṃ tīrthajalaṃ jalāśayān nirgatya nadījalamadhye patati |
	tatra saṃgamatīrthe snānādikaṃ bhavati |
	ayaṃ jalāśayo bhṛṅgpuragaṇe pūrvoktakuṭahārapuragaṇanikaṭavartini yo divalgāsanāmā grāmo 'sti |
	tanmadhye khyātimad bhavati |
	grāmīṇāḥ kāśmīrikāś cāsya tīrthasya sundabhrār iti nāma vadanti |
	tatra bhrār kaśmīrabhāṣāyāṃ devīnāma bhavati |
	ataḥ sundabhrār sundaradevīty arthaḥ |
	asya puragaṇasya bhṛṅggrāmasya ca divalgon iti grāmīṇānām uccaraṇaviṣaye vartate |
	asya grāmasyādhastāt bihū jalan gām iti khyātaṃ grāmadvayaṃ bhavati |
	asya tīrthavarasya śirasi eko vṛkṣaḥ pippalavṛkṣa ivopalakṣaṇībhūto 'pi vartate |
	sandhyākaraṇavelāyāṃ jalaprādurbhāvakāle puṣpākṣatanaivedyādipātanenāpy antardhānaṃ jalam āgacchati |
	tadā jalāśayād eva jalaṃ uddhṛtya snānādikaṃ sarve kurvanti |
	atha dvitīyasandhyākaraṇavelāyāṃ vinītatayā pratīkṣamāṇair janair yadā sthīyate tadā jalaṃ pūrvavad bahir nirgatya saṃgamajalena militvā snānādikaṃ sidhyati |
	ye kecana daṇḍadhāriṇo rājapuruṣāḥ khaḍgādyāyudhādibhis sahaivāvinītavat sandhyākaraṇavelāyāṃ jalāśayasyāsya taṭe 'śucitayaivāgacchanti tān aśucīn avinītāṃś ca dṛṣṭvā jalam adarśanaṃ yāti |
	ataḥ sarvathaivāyaṃ tīrthavaro 'dbhuto mānyaḥ pūjyaś cāsmin deśe khyātatamo 'pi vartate |
	ata eva
children.translated_text: Therefore, during the summer season in the month of <s>Jyaiṣṭha</s>, just as the <s>sandhyā</s> (twilight worship) is performed at dawn, midday, and evening, so too the pilgrimage to this excellent <s>tīrtha</s> (sacred site) is like the <s>sandhyā</s> itself. This water-body is filled with round stones in the middle and on the sides. At the time when, after performing the <s>sandhyā</s>, the water recedes, mice emerge from those very stone crevices and eat the unbroken rice and other offerings thrown by devotees into the water-body for worship. Near this excellent <s>tīrtha</s> are seven water-bodies of the Seven Sages (<s>Saptarṣi</s>). From one of them a small canal also emerges. A small river flows below this mountain <s>tīrtha</s>. During the time of <s>sandhyā</s> performance, the <s>tīrtha</s> water exits the water-body and falls into the river. At that confluence-<s>tīrtha</s>, bathing and other [rites] take place. This water-body is renowned within a village called <s>Divalgā</s>, which is in the <s>Bhṛṅgapura</s> district, situated near the aforementioned <s>Kuṭahāra</s> district. The villagers and Kashmiris call this <s>tīrtha</s> by the name <s>Sundabhrār</s>. There, <s>bhrār</s> in the Kashmiri language means 'goddess.' Therefore <s>Sundabhrār</s> means 'Beautiful Goddess.' The districts of <s>Bhṛṅga</s> village and <s>Divalgon</s> are in the spoken usage of the villagers. Below this village are two villages known as <s>Bihū</s> and <s>Jalangām</s>. On the summit of this excellent <s>tīrtha</s> stands one tree, resembling a <s>pippala</s> tree, serving as a distinguishing mark. During the <s>sandhyā</s> performance, at the time of the water's appearance, even by the throwing of flowers, unbroken rice, food-offerings, and the like, the water disappears. Then, drawing water from the water-body itself, all perform bathing and other rites. Then, during the second <s>sandhyā</s> performance, when people wait with restraint, the water emerges as before and, joining with the confluence water, bathing and other rites are accomplished. Those staff-bearing royal servants who come disrespectfully with swords and other weapons to the bank of this water-body during the <s>sandhyā</s> time in an impure state — seeing such impure and disrespectful persons, the water vanishes from sight. Therefore, in every way this excellent <s>tīrtha</s> is indeed miraculous, revered, and worshipful, and is also the most famous in this land. Therefore —
"The vision of the meritorious and sinful, in positive and negative concomitance" —

children.translated_text: Verse 34, number 6: '<s>Svayambhū</s> (the Self-Arisen).' That sacrificial fire (<s>hutabhuk</s>) which blazes by itself and is not kindled by anyone else is called <s>svayambhū</s> (self-born). Such is this sacrificial fire. In the description of its greatness, it is written that in ancient times, at the prayer of sages and devotees, <s>Śiva</s> manifested his own <s>Kālāgnirudra</s> (the Rudra of the fire of time) form at this very place. Here, everywhere there is desert-land, which is called 'karevā' in the language known as Hindi, and 'uḍar' in the Kashmiri language. This very ground is seen in many places as baked and fissured. From this it is known that this fire does not always emerge from one single place; rather, sometimes it appears in one spot, sometimes in another, and sometimes it arises in yet another location. And the elders say that this fire always manifests at this very place at intervals of more than twelve years, or even longer. Here, pilgrims come and, having purified themselves, clean their own cooking vessels; in those very vessels they put rice and water in appropriate measure; having made a pit-shaped [hole] in the ground scratched out with a piece of wood, they place those vessels in that very heated ground for half a <s>muhūrta</s> (approximately 24 minutes). By the time they remove their vessels from the pits, that food in those cooking vessels is well-cooked — and indeed all people see it as better than food cooked with firewood and other fuel. Then those pilgrims, with that very food, perform <s>śrāddha</s> (ancestral rites) and other ceremonies according to their taste and proper ritual, preceded by the offering of <s>piṇḍas</s> (rice-balls) to their ancestors. Those who wish to perform a <s>homa</s> (fire ritual) place dry wood all around on that same heated ground and produce flames with ghee and the like. In those very flames they perform the <s>homa</s> according to the procedure prescribed in their own <s>gṛhya</s> (domestic ritual) texts. Therefore,
"[The fire] receives the oblation (<s>havis</s>) of those who offer, with arms of flame" —

	asya nicyahaumgrāmasya nikaṭe 'nyad grāmadvayam apy asti |
	tatraikasya nicyahaumsamīpavartino grāmasya rājypaur iti tasyādhastād vartino 'nyasya grāmasya jacyalaur iti te eva grāmīṇāḥ kathayanti |

children.translated_text: thus what <s>Kalhaṇa</s> said also accords [with observation]. For this fire, when kindled, having more abundant flames [than ordinary fire], receives the oblation. The portion of ground where this fire manifests is extremely hot, perceivable even by the touch of a hand and the like. The locally famous name of this place, which both villagers and city-dwellers use, is '<s>Svayam</s>' (Self). This place is in the district called 'Macchepor' in the <s>Krama</s> territory. The villagers at this time call the <s>Krama</s> territory 'Kamrāj,' and this district 'Tapay Macchyapūr.' The village where this fire is [found], the villagers are seen calling 'Nicyahaum.' Near this village of Nicyahaum, there are also two other villages. Of those, the villagers call one village near Nicyahaum 'Rājypaur,' and the other village situated below it 'Jacyalaur.' In these two villages dwell people designated by the word 'rājya' [i.e., Rajput-descended], who are <s>mlecchas</s> (non-Vedic peoples). This village of Nicyahaum is at a distance of twenty <s>krośas</s> (approximately forty miles) from the marvelous place of the fire, from the place of <s>Suyyapura</s>, whose modern name in villagers' pronunciation is 'Sopor.' Although the ground at the fire-associated site in this village is indeed desert, nevertheless on both sides nearby, in the crop fields, the production of crops and the like does indeed occur.
7. <s>Haṃsavāgīśvarī</s>, also known by the alternative name <s>Bheḍā Devī</s>

children.translated_text: Verse 35, number 7: '<s>Sarasvatī</s> in the form of a swan (<s>haṃsa</s>).' The Goddess destroys the darkness characterized by ignorance (<s>avidyā</s>) — thus '<s>haṃsa</s>' means the supreme Self (<s>Paramātman</s>). She who has that form, that is, that power (<s>śakti</s>). Such is this <s>Sarasvatī</s>, the presiding deity of speech (<s>Vāgadhiṣṭhātrī</s>), known as <s>Vāgīśvarī</s> (the Lady of Speech) — she is <s>Sarasvatī</s> in the form of a <s>haṃsa</s>. She is seen by all at the peak, the summit, of the mountain called <s>Bheḍa</s>, which is sanctified by the emergence of the river known as <s>Bhṛṅgī</s>, which flows with great force. Here, on top of the mountain, there is a lake (<s>sara</s>). That very lake, which exists as the abode of the swan <s>Vāgīśvarī</s>, remains in all respects [unchanged]. The river that flows through the township called <s>Bhṛṅga</s> is known as '<s>Bhṛṅgī</s>' — it flows at the foot of the aforementioned mountain. The villagers pronounce the township name as '<s>Bhṛṅg</s>.' Of the village situated below that <s>Bheḍa</s> mountain, they also give the name '<s>Bhiḍar</s>' by the word '<s>Bheḍa</s>' itself. But modern residents of that village call that lake on <s>Bheḍa</s> mountain the '<s>Kātyāyanī Taḍāga</s>' (Pond of <s>Kātyāyanī</s>). There, '<s>Kātyāyanī</s>' means the goddess — that is, this is the pond (<s>taḍāga</s>), the lake (<s>sarovara</s>), of this very swan <s>Vāgīśvarī</s>. Of this '<s>Kātyāyanī Taḍāga</s>,' they pronounce the name as '<s>Kāntrāg</s>' in their own language, through the fault of corruption. There, '<s>Kān</s>' is from <s>Kātyāyanī</s>, and '<s>trāg</s>' means <s>taḍāga</s> (pond). However, on that mountain, the lake is at the summit, and at the foot of the mountain, a river also flows. Therefore:
"The Goddess, on the peak of <s>Bheḍa</s> mountain, herself [present] in the purity of the emergence of the <s>Gaṅgā</s>,
is seen within the lake where <s>Sarasvatī</s> [appears] in the form of a swan" —

In this village called <s>Bhiḍar</s>, there is one stone image of the Goddess in the middle of the water of this river. children.translated_text:
Verse 36, Number 8: <s>Nandikṣetra</s>.
He who delights and brings joy to all his devotees is <s>Nandī</s>, that is, <s>Śiva</s>. His field, his sacred site (<s>tīrtha</s>), is <s>Nandikṣetra</s>. Alternatively, the <s>gaṇa</s> (attendant) named <s>Nandī</s>, who is <s>Śiva</s>'s follower — the place that became a <s>tīrtha</s> by his grace is itself <s>Nandikṣetra</s>.
In ancient times, on the mountain called <s>Haramukuṭa</s>, <s>Pārvatī</s> was in seclusion. At the base of that mountain, in the <s>Dhāra</s> region, [<s>Śiva</s>] stationed his attendant named <s>Nandī</s>, the chief of the <s>gaṇas</s>. From that very time, <s>Nandikṣetra</s> came into being there.
Accordingly, in the <s>Bhṛṅgīśasaṃhitā</s>, in the section describing the greatness of the pilgrimage to <s>Haramukuṭagaṅgā</s>: Once, <s>Pārvatī</s> saw the <s>Gaṅgā</s> surging forth from the matted crown (<s>kaparda</s>) called the <s>jaṭāmukuṭa</s> on <s>Śiva</s>'s head. Then, seeing her co-wife, <s>Śiva</s>'s beloved, with the jealousy of a rival wife and with eyes crooked with anger, <s>Pārvatī</s> said to <s>Śiva</s>: 'Release this rival of mine!' Then, though <s>Śiva</s> entreated her in many ways, <s>Pārvatī</s> held fast to her insistence in the manner of: 'If I am your dearest, then you must certainly abandon her.' And again, <s>Śiva</s>, overwhelmed by devotion to <s>Pārvatī</s>, at the time when he released that <s>Gaṅgā</s> from his matted crown, at that very time the name <s>Haramukuṭagaṅgā</s> arose for that <s>Gaṅgā</s> — because the <s>Gaṅgā</s> that flowed forth from <s>Hara</s>'s (<s>Śiva</s>'s) crown is <s>Haramukuṭagaṅgā</s>. Alternatively, having fallen from <s>Hara</s>'s crown, because she flowed upon the earth with extreme swiftness, she is [called] <s>Mukuṭagaṅgā</s>.
Then <s>Śiva</s> made a request to <s>Pārvatī</s> preceded by great respect: 'O Goddess, this <s>Gaṅgā</s> whom I have released from my head at your command — I shall bear her again.' Hearing such words of <s>Śiva</s>, the Goddess, filled with great anger, abandoned <s>Śiva</s> and, to display her self-respect, ascended the mountain called <s>Haramukuṭa</s>, which was her place of dwelling. At the time of ascending, she gave this order to <s>Nandin</s>, the guardian of that mountain and <s>Śiva</s>'s chief attendant: 'O <s>Nandin</s>, I shall remain alone secretly on this mountain peak for some time. Therefore, you who stand below at the entrance of this mountain must act in such a way that no one else sees me who am in seclusion. Furthermore, if someone comes wishing to enter near me, entry here must not be given to anyone.'
Then, having received such an order from the Goddess, while <s>Nandī</s> stood immovable as a rock, blocking entry, <s>Śiva</s> too, searching for the Goddess everywhere, arrived at the foot of <s>Haramukuṭa</s>. There, even though <s>Śiva</s> saw <s>Nandin</s>, his own attendant, standing firm as a rock, when he wished to enter near the Goddess and turned to ascend the mountain, <s>Nandin</s> [said]: 'The Goddess who stays in seclusion has not given permission to ascend here. Therefore, you may not ascend.' Thus blocked and prevented, <s>Śiva</s> himself, though admonishing <s>Nandin</s> many times, seeing him not budging again and again due to his own stubbornness, that god, with eyes crooked with extreme anger, cursed him thus: 'You fool! Since you disrespect even me, the lord of this mountain and of the Goddess who dwells on this mountain, from today you shall become one of dull intellect, in stone form, at the base of this mountain, through my extremely harsh curse.'
Here, in the Sanskrit language, the letters <s>la</s> and <s>ḍa</s> being equivalent in meaning, [<s>jaḍarūpa</s> means] 'you shall become water-form' (<s>jalarūpa</s>).
Hearing this curse-fire issuing from <s>Śiva</s>'s lotus-mouth, <s>Nandī</s> too thought in his mind: 'Ah! He is obeying the command of <s>Śivā</s> (<s>Pārvatī</s>), <s>Śiva</s>'s other half. How could <s>Śiva</s> have cursed me thoughtlessly and in vain?' Thinking thus, with a mind prepared to counter-curse his own lord, he spoke thus: 'Since you, my lord, have given me a curse without deliberation, even though I was under another's command, you too, by my curse, from today shall be in the form of <s>Kāla</s> (Time/Black), here near my water-body.' The meaning is: 'You shall be a water-body with dark-colored water here.'
Therefore, from that time onward, on <s>Haramukuṭa</s> mountain, a pair of water-bodies near each other came into being — one became a sacred fire-<s>tīrtha</s> through <s>Śiva</s>'s boon-granting. Of these, one is named <s>Nandikṣetra</s> and the other is named <s>Kālakṣetra</s>. Even in modern times, these two water-bodies are referred to by these very names, and white water and black water are visible to the eyes of pilgrims. But —
In <s>Nandikṣetra</s> (the field of Nandi), in the celestial temple, [offerings] dedicated to the sky-dwellers (gods),
where even today the drops of worship-sandal (<s>pūjācandanabindu</s>) are visible.

children.translated_text: Thus what the <s>paṇḍita</s> <s>Kalhaṇa</s> wrote in his own book — in modern times, due to the absence of temples and the like, the seeing of sandal drops and so forth does not at all correspond [to observation]. From this it is known that all of that must have existed in ancient times. The pair of water-bodies mentioned by him is called by the two names 'Nund Kol' in the Kashmiri village language, as spoken by all people. This pair of sacred sites (<s>tīrtha</s>) is situated on the border-land of the township called <s>Lahara</s>, near the <s>Haramukuṭa Gaṅgā</s> (Harmukh glacier river). On the pilgrimage route to <s>Haramukuṭa Gaṅgā</s>, the vision of this very pair of sacred sites occurs first. After that, the pilgrims arrive at the bank of <s>Mukuṭa Gaṅgā</s>. In the village language, this township is called 'Lārpargaṇa,' and <s>Mukuṭa Gaṅgā</s> is called 'Gaṅgabal' — since 'bal' in the Kashmiri language means 'place,' therefore 'Gaṅgabal' means 'the place of the <s>Gaṅgā</s>.' On this pilgrimage to <s>Haramukuṭa Gaṅgā</s>, the village of <s>Nunar</s>, which is at a distance of seven <s>krośas</s> from the city of <s>Kaśmīra</s> — there the pilgrims, having arrived on the first day, on the second day proceed along the river known by the name <s>Karaṅkanadī</s>, and by that very route they arrive at the village called <s>Rāmarādhan</s>. Up to this village of <s>Rāmarādhan</s>, crop-fields, village trees, and the like are visible everywhere. From this place onward, there are only mountains everywhere. Foremost among them is the mountain called <s>Bharata</s>, whose name in local opinion is 'Bharuth.' Climbing it, the pilgrims proceed. From this very place onward, no village or anything else is to be found all the way to <s>Haramukuṭa Gaṅgā</s>. The trees here are all wild forest trees, visible everywhere. From <s>Bharata</s> mountain up to <s>Haramukuṭa</s>, nowhere are there such trees from which firewood for cooking and other purposes could be taken. However, there is one vine-shaped wood (<s>latākṛti kāṣṭha</s>) of such a nature that, even while moist, when uprooted at that very time, it burns. The Sanskrit name of that wood is <s>vānarendhana</s> ('monkey-fuel'). And thus <s>Kalhaṇa</s> [says]: 'The powerless <s>vānarendhana</s> does not blaze even in contact with fire.' This type of wood, though devoid of flame, nevertheless accomplishes cooking and other functions. In the speech of the villagers, this is called 'Viṭhur' or 'Viṭhar Kāṭh.'
9. <s>Śāradā Devī</s> (The Goddess Śāradā)

children.translated_text: Verse 37, number 9: <s>Śāradā Devī</s>. Here the etymology of the word <s>Śāradā</s>: <s>Śāra</s> means 'a multitude of arrows (<s>bāṇa</s>)'; she who cuts (<s>dyati</s>) the net (<s>jāla</s>) [cast] upon the demons (<s>daitya</s>) is <s>Śāradā</s>. Or alternatively, <s>śāra</s> [means] 'wind,' and it also [means] 'variegated' in the three [genders] — according to the lexicon (<s>kośa</s>). She who destroys (<s>dyati</s>) the illusory form (<s>māyārūpa</s>) of wind (<s>vāyu</s>) is <s>Śāradā</s>. And furthermore: she who gives (<s>dadāti</s>) <s>śāra</s>, that is, variegated and manifold scholarly and artistic knowledge (<s>śāstrīya śilpādika jñāna</s>), is <s>Śāradā</s>. And moreover, through the identity of the letters <s>śa</s> and <s>sa</s>, <s>Śāradā</s> is also <s>Sāradā</s>. There, she who gives <s>sāra</s> — that is, strength, capability, knowledge, excellent things, and the supreme — is <s>Sāradā</s>. Those who behold such a <s>Śāradā Devī</s>, whose nature is illumination — that is, those people who undertake the pilgrimage to the <s>Śāradā</s> sacred site — they, by her grace, assuredly [become] frequented by poets, always honored by poets, and attain the speech (<s>Vāṇī</s>) of Sanskrit, which has the form of <s>Vaikharī</s> (articulated speech). By the blessing of <s>Śāradā</s>, they become poets skilled in the craft of poetry, endowed with poetic power. And furthermore: those who, intent upon the pilgrimage to that sacred site, go there, assuredly also reach the river named <s>Madhumatī</s>. That is, there is one river situated in the middle of the pilgrimage route, famous by the name <s>Madhumatī</s>. Therefore, in the middle of the route, they also encounter it. Therefore —
the river <s>Madhumatī</s> and <s>Vāṇī</s> (Speech/Sarasvatī), frequented by poets.

children.translated_text: Thus what <s>Kalhaṇa</s> said is most fitting. By virtue of the association with this very <s>Śāradā Devī</s>, some people also call this land of <s>Kaśmīra</s> by the name '<s>Śāradāpīṭha</s>' (Seat of <s>Śāradā</s>). In that regard, by the etymology '<s>Śāradā</s>'s <s>pīṭha</s> (seat)' meaning '<s>Śāradā</s>'s abode,' this land, which has become the seat of <s>Śāradā</s>, is appropriately designated by the word '<s>Śāradāpīṭha</s>.' Here at the site of <s>Śāradā Devī</s>, there is a water-body in the shape of a <s>kuṇḍa</s> (ritual pool). Above it there is one such large stone slab. By which that entire <s>kuṇḍa</s> appears concealed from view and is thus in every way [hidden]. Here on the bright eighth (<s>śuklāṣṭamī</s>) of the month of <s>Bhādrapada</s>, a pilgrimage is undertaken by pilgrims. And likewise, the completion of the entire ritual sequence of <s>śrāddha</s> (ancestral rites), <s>homa</s> (fire ritual), and other ceremonies, preceded by shaving, also takes place here. From the city of <s>Kaśmīra</s>, the <s>Śāradā</s> <s>tīrtha</s> (sacred site) is reached in eight stages of travel, known as '<s>paḍāv</s>.' The path is extremely difficult and mostly through water, yet is traversed in all ways by the pilgrims. This site of <s>Śāradā</s>, having crossed the entire <s>Krama</s> territory, is situated at the place known as '<s>Drauv</s>' which lies at the front. In the Kashmiri language, people call this site of <s>Śāradā</s> by the name '<s>Śārad</s>.' This <s>Drauv</s> district has connections through land with <s>Karaṇāv</s>, <s>Mujapharābād</s>, <s>Gilgith</s>, and many other regions situated on the borders of <s>Kaśmīra</s>. The people dwelling in this place are known by the name 'Gujjer.' They are seen speaking a language spoken in the land of the Five Rivers (<s>Pañcanada</s>, Punjab). The pilgrimage to this place involves travel by two routes.
10. <s>Cakradhara</s>

children.translated_text: Verse 38, number 10: <s>Cakrabhṛt</s> (Disc-Bearer). He who bears, that is, holds the disc (<s>cakra</s>) is <s>Cakrabhṛt</s> — <s>Viṣṇu</s>. Here, since the root '<s>bhṛ</s>' and the root '<s>dhṛ</s>' are synonymous in the sense of 'holding,' <s>Cakrabhṛt</s> is indeed the same as <s>Cakradhara</s>. In ancient times, it is said, when the entire earth was oppressed by a state of disorder due to various kinds of <s>daityas</s> (demons) who were troublesome to the gods, maddened by boons obtained through the power of their austerities, causing various calamities, and by that very reason burdening the earth — then she, the Earth, approached the gods weeping and spoke thus: 'O gods, these demons, proud through their boons, are tormenting me in every way. What shall I do? How shall I continue to exist?' Then those gods, having heard the pitiful lamentation of that Earth Goddess (<s>Bhūdevī</s>), and having consoled that goddess with words inspiring confidence, themselves also having become distressed, most speedily went together with that Earth Goddess to take refuge with the <s>Bhagavān</s> <s>Viṣṇu</s>, the refuge of the entire world. Having arrived there, those gods praised that Lord with many meaningful hymns of praise and spoke of the desire [behind] their coming thus: 'O Lord, we all, as well as this Earth, being tormented by wicked <s>daityas</s> and being in extreme distress now, have come to you, the <s>Bhagavān</s>, for refuge. Therefore, you should arrange for the slaying of the demons so that we, together with this goddess, may obtain peace.' Then the <s>Bhagavān</s>, having heard the wish of the gods, placing those gods and that Earth Goddess before him, went to the world of <s>Śiva</s> (<s>Śivaloka</s>) for the purpose of propitiating <s>Śiva</s>. There, that <s>Bhagavān</s>, having propitiated <s>Śiva</s> — who is indeed his own form — together with those gods, through appropriate worship such as hymns of praise, and having also communicated to <s>Śiva</s> the purpose of his coming, at that very time obtained from that [<s>Śiva</s>], who was duly satisfied, the disc called <s>Sudarśana</s>, which destroys hosts of demons. From that time onward, by that very <s>Viṣṇu</s>, the disc-bearer (<s>Cakradhara</s>), the task of slaying demons stationed everywhere was commenced. For the very purpose of slaying the demons situated in <s>Kaśmīra</s>, <s>Viṣṇu</s> established his residence in this place situated near <s>Vijayeśvara</s>. By the association of that very place with the aforementioned <s>Cakradhara</s>, the name '<s>Cakradhara</s>' was born. But villagers nowadays pronounce the name of that <s>Cakradhara</s> as 'Cakadhar' in the Kashmiri language. And the modern name of that <s>Vijayeśvara</s>, near which this Cakadhar is situated, is 'Vijyabhror.' This Vijyabhror as well as this Cakadhar are situated within the southern district, which in modern villagers' parlance is named 'Dacchunpor Pargaṇa' (Southern District). Here there is a river named <s>Lambodarī</s>, which in the villagers' language is now called 'Lidar.' Of that very river, there is a left side and a southern side. Those two are indeed designated as the 'southern side' and the 'left side.' There, in the Kashmiri language, the left side has the name 'Khourpor Pargaṇa' and the southern side has the name 'Dacchunpor Pargaṇa' — these are the two names. Near this Cakadhar there is another village whose name is 'Simathan.' It too exists here. This Cakadhar now appears like a small mountain. This place called Cakadhar is situated on the bank on the southern side of the river <s>Vitastā</s>. Some say: beneath this Cakadhar there is a great subterranean passage. In former times, those who used to go back and forth by that path would invariably, by constant divine grace, obtain ancient coins, otherwise known as <s>dīnāras</s> (gold coins) and the like. Even in modern times, any man, however extremely destitute, who relies on the deity with extreme devotion and goes to this place Cakadhar, regarding this very <s>Cakradhara</s>, with the desire for wealth — he too invariably obtains some wealth and the like. This place is situated at a distance of fourteen <s>krośas</s> to the east of the city of <s>Kaśmīra</s>. For those who come to the city of <s>Kaśmīra</s> from <s>Anantanāga</s>, this place comes into view after crossing merely three <s>krośas</s>. From <s>Vijayeśvara</s>, this is at a distance of only one <s>krośa</s>. At the foot of this <s>Cakradhara</s>, there are also <s>cīrā</s> (chinar) trees native to <s>Kaśmīra</s>. Peace.

children.translated_text: Verse 38, number 11: '<s>Vijayeśa</s>.' He who especially conquers among all the hosts of gods, who exists in supreme eminence, is '<s>Vijaya</s>' (the Victorious One). Alternatively, he who conquers or defeats the various hosts of <s>daityas</s> (demons) and others is '<s>Vijaya</s>.' And he who is '<s>Īśa</s>' — he who rules, who bestows sovereignty — is '<s>Īśa</s>' (the Lord). <s>Vijaya</s> himself who is <s>Īśa</s> is '<s>Vijayeśa</s>.' The image of <s>Śiva</s> situated at this place is designated by the word '<s>Vijayeśa</s>,' since the image designated by the word '<s>Īśa</s>' (Lord) is everywhere recited as being that of <s>Śiva</s> alone. This place named <s>Vijayeśvara</s> is inferred to have been most famous by this very name from a very ancient time. For here one finds only those who performed the work of restoration of the dilapidated [temple] and the like; but the name of the original builder is for the most part not ascertained. Because the <s>paṇḍita</s> <s>Kalhaṇa</s> too writes in verse 105 of the first <s>taraṅga</s> (wave) of his own <s>Rājataraṅgiṇī</s>. Thus:
Having removed the dilapidated plaster-made [enclosure] of the glorious <s>Vijayeśa</s>,
by him a stone enclosure-wall was caused to be made, pure and spotless.

children.translated_text: — that is, by King <s>Aśoka</s> — this is the meaning. Here, by the mention of removing the lime-plastered (<s>sudhāmaya</s>) enclosure wall and the mention of constructing a stone enclosure wall, it is understood that King <s>Aśoka</s> [merely renovated what existed] previously, and that the great antiquity of this site is confirmed by its prior existence. In the Persian books, some write that this site called <s>Vijayeśvara</s> was established by King <s>Surendra</s>, who was even more ancient than King <s>Aśoka</s>. Others say that it was built by the queen known as <s>Īśānadevī</s>, the wife of King <s>Jalauka</s>, the ruler of the earth who came after the kings <s>Surendra</s> and <s>Aśoka</s>. Some are seen writing in their own books that the initial construction of this site was done by King <s>Aśoka</s> himself. However, none of the three stated views seems most consistent or proper. For, in the <s>Rājataraṅgiṇī</s>, in the description of King <s>Surendra</s> narrated from the ninety-first verse of the first <s>taraṅga</s> (chapter), the name <s>Vijayeśvara</s> does not appear at all in the entire [passage]. Therefore, the claim that it was established by <s>Surendra</s> is also unsupported. As for those who say that this site was built by Queen <s>Īśānadevī</s> of King <s>Jalauka</s> — in the <s>Rājataraṅgiṇī</s>, in the history of King <s>Jalauka</s> narrated from the one-hundred-and-seventh verse of the first <s>taraṅga</s>, and within that, in the history of the aforementioned queen — nowhere is the name <s>Vijayeśvara</s> to be found. Therefore that too appears unsupported. As for those who, considering King <s>Aśoka</s> himself to be the founder of <s>Vijayeśvara</s>, write in their books that <s>Aśoka</s> is the founder of <s>Vijayeśvara</s> and so forth — they, having obtained from the <s>Rājataraṅgiṇī</s> itself [only the account of] removing the dilapidated lime-plastered wall and constructing a new stone wall, and knowing this to be directly [only] a work of renovation and restoration, write thus. Therefore, their view too appears unconsidered. For there is a great difference between a founder and a restorer of what is dilapidated. In truth, since the name <s>Vijayeśvara</s> is nowhere visible even at the beginning of the <s>Rājataraṅgiṇī</s>, it is known that even <s>paṇḍita</s> <s>Kalhaṇa</s> did not directly know the founder of this site, since even he, in describing the assemblage of kings prior to King <s>Aśoka</s>, did not mention this matter at all. Therefore, the great antiquity of this site shines forth well. Here, on the left bank of the <s>Vitastā</s> (Jhelum river), as observed along the route coming from <s>Anantanāga</s>, stands this very edifice called <s>Vijayeśvara</s>. And the elders say: in this site there has always been a deity-temple (<s>devatāgāra</s>) built of stone, serving as the main temple. However, the stone-built structure that is visible in the present time was accomplished by the late King <s>Śrī Raṇavīrasiṃha</s>, who attained a good destiny in the celestial world, the ruler of <s>Kaśmīra</s>, <s>Jammu</s>, and many other territories, who, with great effort, enormous exertion, and expenditure of thousands of <s>rūpakas</s> (rupees) over many years, accomplished it. In this temple there is now an image of <s>Śiva</s>. For the maintenance of its worship and other services, the king has also established one village under the designation of <s>agrahāra</s> (a grant for the hosting of guests and worship). The villagers, understanding this temple to be made by <s>Haricandra</s>, call it 'Haricandrājan Mandir' ('Temple of King Haricandra') in their own Kashmiri language, and call the stairway path descending from the river bank to the water 'Haricandrājun Yārabal.' The meaning of the first name is 'the temple made by <s>Haricandra</s>.' The meaning of the second name is 'the stairway path established by <s>Haricandra</s>.' For in the Kashmiri language, all stairway paths are designated by the word '<s>yārabal</s>.' In the Kashmiri language, '<s>yār</s>' is a friend's name. '<s>Bal</s>' means the place of those very friends — because in the land of <s>Kaśmīra</s>, everyone goes to the river bank for bathing in the early morning. Therefore, those who are mutual friends meet there. For this very reason, the name '<s>yārabal</s>' (friends' place) became established for this river bank. Here, going just a few steps above <s>Vijayeśvara</s>, there are many trees called '<s>chinār</s>' in the common language, which in the scholarly language are designated by the term '<s>chāyāvṛkṣa</s>' (shade trees). Likewise, on the opposite bank facing <s>Vijayeśvara</s> across the <s>Vitastā</s>, there are also many of the aforementioned trees. And people say that these two tree-grove-encircled places are a pair of gardens of an ancient king. These two gardens have the name 'Pādaśāhī Bāg' (Imperial Garden) in village parlance. Likewise, the name of this site, in local usage, is 'Vijyabhror.' Here, near <s>Vijayeśvara</s> itself, there is also a ferry (<s>pratara</s>) for crossing from one bank to the other of the river, which they call 'Vijyabhrori Kadal' (the ferry of Vijyabhror). In the garden grounds mentioned above, brickwork and similar remains of ancient royal construction are still visible even today. Blessings.
12. <s>Ādikeśava</s>

children.translated_text:
Verse 38, Number 12: <s>Ādikeśava</s>. The etymology of this <s>Keśava</s>: He who pervades <s>ka</s> (<s>Brahmā</s>), <s>a</s> (<s>Viṣṇu</s>), and <s>Īśa</s> (<s>Śiva</s>) within himself, illuminating them and covering those who are illuminated — he is <s>Keśava</s>. And he who exists even at the very beginning of the creation of this entire world — he is <s>Ādikeśava</s>. That is, the one who performs the actions of creation, preservation, and destruction of the world. The primordial, eternal Supreme Self (<s>Paramātman</s>), <s>Viṣṇu</s> — this very one is designated by the word <s>Ādikeśava</s>.
Among all the various deity images situated in this province of <s>Kaśmīra</s>, since this very image of the Lord <s>Viṣṇu</s> is the foremost here, it has come to be called by the word <s>Ādikeśava</s>. By the very existence of this <s>Ādikeśava</s>, the name <s>Ādyāvani</s> ('Primordial Earth') has become attached to this district. Therein, <s>ādya</s> means 'at the beginning,' and <s>avani</s> means 'earth' — that is the meaning. Since by the establishment of <s>Ādikeśava</s>, this very land became the foremost among all lands, it came to be called <s>Ādyāvani</s>.
In the opinion of some, when formerly this land was in the state of being a lake, when this region was completely flooded by waters surging from all sides — waters characterized by eddies, hollows, and various transformations, waters that were always filling the lake by virtue of this land's quality of being nourished by rivers — at that time, by the grace of the gods satisfied by the power of the sage <s>Kaśyapa</s>'s austerities, when the water was made into dry land for the purpose of establishing dwelling regions, at the manifestation of earth-nature, it was right here in <s>Ādyāvani</s> that dry land first became visible. Therefore, this district is designated as <s>Ādyāvani</s> ('Primordial Earth') — such is also [said].
Therein, the word <s>Ādyāvani</s> means: that which exists at the beginning, and which is earth — the primordial earth. And in this <s>Ādyāvani</s> district there exists a water-body known by this name, in which the image designated by the word <s>Keśava</s> can now be seen thus: the upper part is of expanded form, while the lower part is of contracted form. This water-body is round in shape, like the previously described <s>Sandhyādevī</s> water-body. The villagers now call the village where this <s>Ādikeśava</s> image-water-body is located by the name <s>Phrasal</s>. Furthermore, they call the district of this village <s>Āḍvin</s>. This water-body also has the name <s>Keśavanāg</s>, famous in the local language. Therein, <s>Keśava</s> refers to this very <s>Ādikeśava</s>, and <s>nāg</s> means 'water-body' — because in the land of <s>Kaśmīra</s>, all water-bodies are designated by the word <s>nāg</s>. Near this village known as <s>Phrasal</s>, there is also another village named <s>Ārvañ</s>. Therefore, some villagers say the combined name <s>Phrasal Ārvañ</s>. The <s>Āḍvin</s> district, the location of this water-body, lies in the terrain below the <s>Devar</s> district.
13. <s>Īśāna</s>

children.translated_text: Verse 38, Number 13: <s>Īśāna</s>. He who rules (<s>īṣṭe</s>) in all the world and exercises sovereignty (<s>aiśvarya</s>) — he is <s>Īśāna</s>. <s>Śiva</s>, who is the overlord of all the hosts of gods, who abides in the world wielding prosperity and sovereignty, and who is the master of all riches and powers — he is designated by the word <s>Īśāna</s>. Since the words <s>Śiva</s> and <s>Īśāna</s> are synonymous, this is a <s>Śiva</s> image at the described place — that is the meaning. Alternatively, the guru of the king called <s>Sandhimān</s> or <s>Sandhimati</s>, described in the second <s>taraṅga</s> (wave/chapter) of the <s>Rājataraṅgiṇī</s> composed by the learned <s>Kalhaṇa</s>, by whose grace even the dead king <s>Sandhimati</s> regained life — he was named <s>Īśāna</s>, and therefore by his name too this <s>Śiva</s> image located here came to be called by the word <s>Īśāna</s>. Accordingly, in verse one hundred and thirty-seven of the second <s>taraṅga</s> of <s>Kalhaṇa</s>'s <s>Rājataraṅgiṇī</s> —
Having made [the shrine of] <s>Sandhīśvara</s> in the cremation ground (<s>pitṛkānana</s>) [associated with] the joining of the body (<s>dehasandhāna</s>),

children.translated_text: Although known by the name '<s>Īśeśvara</s>,' it came to be famous by the name of that very devotee <s>Īśāna</s> himself. Even though before the time of <s>Īśāna</s>, this place already possessed extreme sanctity and great eminence through the manifestation of a <s>Śiva</s> image, nevertheless, through the revelation of <s>Īśāna</s>'s most extraordinary deeds, it attained complete fame in every respect. Here, in the second <s>taraṅga</s> (chapter), beginning from the sixty-fifth verse, the one to be described is named <s>Jayendra</s>, the son of King <s>Vijaya</s>. His minister named <s>Sandhimati</s>, the most excellent among the wise, was formerly a disciple of <s>Īśāna</s>. Then, people told that king — who was fickle-eared like a maddened elephant — 'This <s>Sandhimati</s>, your minister, is amazingly powerful and exceedingly wealthy in every respect; therefore, suspicion of usurpation of the kingdom and the like must be entertained regarding him,' and so forth. For this very reason, the deceived king harbored enmity and anger even toward that wise minister. Then, the king, his former affection forgotten due to that enmity, reduced the minister to lifelong poverty, first by barring him from entry into his court and then by confiscating all his property — all without cause. Even though he obtained such a wretched condition, that minister did not consider it painful, [seeing] his loss of royal duties and the like as an opportunity gained for unobstructed worship of <s>Śiva</s>. Then, by the force of future destiny, the very prophecy that 'The kingdom shall be <s>Sandhimati</s>'s' suddenly spread from house to house. And so, in the seventy-fourth verse of the second <s>taraṅga</s>:
Then, by the greatness of the future event, [the prophecy] spread from house to house:
'The kingdom shall be <s>Sandhimati</s>'s in the future' — [such was] the speech (<s>Sarasvatī</s>), though unheard [by anyone in particular].

Thereupon, that king, upon hearing such a voice as described above, knowing that 'such a voice does not arise suddenly without cause, therefore it must necessarily be inspired by the gods and such,' and having become greatly frightened, placed that minister in prison.
	There, with his feet tormented by cruel fetters and having become emaciated from that very [suffering], ten years came to completion.
	Those very ten years constituted the remaining lifespan of <s>Jayendra</s>, the king and master of <s>Sandhimati</s>; then, afflicted by disease from sitting without a son, and excessively tormented by anxiety along with his mother, while desiring to die, he internally experienced a great burning.
	In just this manner, being scorched by that blazing fire of hatred toward the minister, burning day and night, that king considered no remedy for what was destined to happen other than the killing of that minister.
	Alas! The means that men who consider themselves wise devise for concealing a future event — that very means, prevented [from its intended purpose], becomes by fate the instrument of that [destined] event.
	Just as when fate, by its own command, wishes to bestow incomparable power upon even a tiny spark of fire resting upon a pile of wood,
	then whoever, not knowing the force of fate, endeavors to extinguish that aforementioned spark about to receive great power — for that person, fate causes the delusion of mistaking a pot of ghee for a pot of water, [the ghee being] melted by heat.
	Now, the very moment the king commanded the executioners to kill the minister, at that very moment <s>Sandhimati</s> was impaled upon a stake by them and put to death.
	Then too, when that minister was impaled upon the stake, from that king first the thorn of suffering from anxiety about the minister departed,
	and afterward his life also departed.
	Now, upon hearing of the killing of his own disciple who had been thus slain, even the self-controlled guru of that [minister], known by the name <s>Īśāna</s>, became inwardly pained in his mind.
	Thereupon, for the purpose of performing the final rites of the funeral pyre for his well-disciplined disciple at the time of death, that <s>Īśāna</s> came to the very cremation ground where <s>Sandhimati</s> had met his death.
	There, <s>Īśāna</s>, having taken hold of his own disciple at the very base of that stake, saw only the remaining bones, with a bone fragment being forcibly dragged from below by wolves.
	And having seen [this], overwhelmed by immense grief, crying out 'Alas, my child! I live only to see such a condition of yours!' and warding off the howling wolves from the skeleton impaled on that stake, he led [it away].
	Then, as <s>Īśāna</s> was preparing to perform the proper final rites, he read this verse inscribed by fate on the forehead-plate of his own disciple.
	Namely:
Poverty for as long as one lives, imprisonment for ten years,

children.translated_text: Thus. Then that guru, having understood the true meaning of the three quarters of the aforementioned verse, became filled with curiosity about the fourth quarter whose meaning was necessarily to be witnessed, and thought in his mind: 'How will this come to pass?' Then, reflecting upon the inconceivable power of <s>Śakti</s>, by which formerly <s>Arjuna</s>, <s>Parīkṣit</s>, <s>Kaca</s>, and others, being dead, had obtained life again — that very power which accomplishes the impossible — and praising the god who is unobstructed and supremely bold in all accomplishments, intent upon witnessing the fulfillment of the future event, he took up residence in that very cremation ground (<s>śmaśāna</s>) and guarded that skeleton. Then one night at midnight, that <s>Īśāna</s>, lying awake with that very wondrous contemplation, first suddenly smelled a divine incense fragrance and heard the sounds of various instruments — <s>ḍamaru</s> (drum), <s>gharāṭa</s> (rattle), and others. Then, upon hearing the sound, as he opened his eyes against the enemy of darkness, he saw a circle of <s>yoginīs</s> resplendent with a halo of light, assembled at that very cremation ground. Then, just as those <s>yoginīs</s> were about to uncover that skeleton, his guru, sword in hand, came to that cremation ground out of fear [for the skeleton]. Having arrived, concealed behind a tree, he saw that skeleton lying in the <s>maṇḍala</s> (ritual circle), all its limbs being worshipped by those hosts of <s>yoginīs</s>. When those <s>yoginīs</s> — whose deity is wine, who desired union with the supreme bridegroom — found no other bridegroom, that very skeleton appeared radiant to the watching [guru]. Then they, placing their own limbs one by one upon it in an instant, and bringing from somewhere the beauty of a man, made it complete-limbed. And again, the <s>yoginīs</s>, by the power of yoga, drew from somewhere the subtle body (<s>puryaṣṭaka</s>) that had been wandering without entering any other form, and established it in that skeleton of <s>Sandhimati</s>. Then that <s>Sandhimati</s>, as if awakened from sleep, anointed by them with divine unguents, assuming the leadership of the circle (<s>cakranāyakatva</s>), enjoyed pleasures and other delights with them as he wished. Then, as the night was dawning, that <s>Īśāna</s>, apprehensive and afraid that the limbs and other portions bestowed by those <s>yoginīs</s> might be taken away again, with steady resolve — for the purpose of protecting [<s>Sandhimati</s>] — when he came to that very place [making] a cry, that very host of <s>yoginīs</s> swiftly vanished. And as those <s>yoginīs</s> disappeared, their voice was heard by him thus: 'O <s>Īśāna</s>, do not fear! For by this deed of ours, there is no loss of limbs. In this matter, there is also no deception. On the contrary, this one, being joined with a divine body by our boon, shall become a king known by the name <s>Sandhimat</s>, and again, by his nobility, he shall become famous on earth by the name <s>Āryarāja</s> (Noble King).' Then that <s>Sandhimati</s>, wearing divine garments, divine ornaments, and a garland, having regained his memory of former [lives], bowed down and saluted his guru. Then that king, having conversed with his guru about the essencelessness of <s>saṃsāra</s> (worldly existence) and [the nature of] consciousness, consenting to that [counsel], with some difficulty, became dispassionate [yet] agreed to the administration of the kingdom. Thus it has been described — the immeasurable service of that guru is the chief cause in the founding and so forth of the site known as <s>Īśeśvara</s>. Although formerly <s>Śiva</s>, known as <s>Mahādeva</s>, was also present at this place, nevertheless even today the fame [of the site] is borne by the name of that very <s>Īśāna</s>. The name of this site is now <s>Guptagaṅgā</s> (Hidden Gaṅgā), known throughout the entire world. There, since the <s>Gaṅgā</s> was hidden (<s>guptā</s>, concealed) by <s>Mahādeva</s>, this name '<s>Guptagaṅgā</s>' is apt. The <s>Gaṅgā</s> was hidden by <s>Mahādeva</s> who had ascended the mountain called <s>Mahādeva</s> near this site. Every year, at the <s>saṃkrānti</s> (solar transit) in the month of <s>Vaiśākha</s>, all Kashmiris — young and old — come to bathe, regarding the <s>Gaṅgā</s> situated here as the <s>Guptagaṅgā</s>. People also say the name of this site is now '<s>Īśabhrār</s>.' There, '<s>Īśa</s>' means <s>Īśāna</s>, and '<s>bhrār</s>' means deity — because in the Kashmiri language, the two well-known words '<s>bhror</s>' and '<s>bhrār</s>' are found to have the meanings of 'god' and 'goddess' respectively. Among them, '<s>bhror</s>' means 'god' and '<s>bhrār</s>' means 'goddess.' Furthermore, since the word <s>devatā</s> is feminine in the <s>śāstra</s> (grammatical science), it is designated as feminine by '<s>bhrār</s>' in the language as well. The villagers, through phonetic corruption (<s>apabhraṃśa</s>) of the word '<s>īśabhrār</s>,' say 'Iśavar.' Furthermore, the township (<s>puragaṇa</s>) in which this site is situated is called 'Phākpargaṇa.' This township is at a distance of three <s>krośas</s> from the city of <s>Kaśmīra</s>. Travel to and from here is by water route in boats, and also by land route with horses and such. This site is at a distance of a quarter of a <s>krośa</s> from [the place] called <s>Niśāt Vāga</s>. Here there is one water-body, with cool water, quadrangular in shape, inside. Furthermore, another such water-body exists on the outer side of that inner water-body. Between the two water-bodies, a small enclosure wall made of bricks, stones, and the like is still visible today as a remnant. However, bathing and other practices take place only at the outer water-body. At the inner one, only worship and the like is performed by all. Above this water-body, a temple built by an ancient king is still visible today, unruined throughout, recognizable by its very form. The local people and other elders say: 'This temple (<s>devālaya</s>) was built by King <s>Sandhimati</s> for the sake of his guru.' In the <s>Mandirasaṃgraha</s> (Collection of Temples) and other [records] too, <s>Sandhimati</s> is known as the founder of this site. Above this site there is also another mountain. And thus this place appears at the foot of the mountain. On this mountain, at some distance, there is also a <s>tīrtha</s> (sacred site) called <s>Gopītīrtha</s>. The villagers, through phonetic corruption, call it 'Gupatrath.' A few steps below the <s>Īśāna</s> <s>tīrtha</s>, there is also a cave. Near that cave, there is also a house of <s>Vaiṣṇava</s> <s>Brāhmaṇas</s> designated by the word '<s>sāhib</s>.' Those <s>Brāhmaṇas</s> never eat meat or the like. Here there is also a temple begun by a modern king that remains half-completed. This pair of water-bodies is now enclosed by walls on all four sides.

Verse 86, number 14: <s>Lolora</s> or <s>Lolara</s> in the account of King <s>Lava</s> described beginning from the eighty-fourth verse.
	Therein, the etymology of <s>Lolora</s>:
	The <s>lolas</s> are those of fickle mind; those who give (<s>rānti</s>) are <s>rās</s>, meaning givers.
	Those who are not givers are <s>arās</s>, non-givers.
	The place where both the fickle (<s>lola</s>) and the non-givers (<s>arā</s>) dwell — that is <s>Lolora</s>.
	Alternatively, '<s>la</s>' is known from the treatises of earlier authorities as [denoting] 'remainder' and 'fear,' according to the single-syllable lexicon; '<s>la</s>' [means] remainder and fear — and since this region is situated at the periphery (<s>prānta</s>) of this territory, in the sense of being the remainder, and since it is also full of fear due to the extremely remote, desolate, cavern-filled and other paths;
	But solely by the charm of its location, '<s>ra</s>' means 'one who gives pleasure' — thus it is also <s>Lolora</s>.
	Now, the etymology of the second name <s>Lolara</s>:
	That which is restless (<s>lola</s>) due to the diverse modes of trees, creepers, shrubs, water, land, and the like — that is <s>lola</s>.
	That which gives (<s>ra</s>) the pleasure of delight through its exceeding charm — that is <s>ra</s>.
	Being <s>lola</s> and [a giver of] <s>ra</s> (pleasure) — it is <s>Lolara</s>.
	Since in this region an exceedingly wondrous city was built by that king named <s>Lava</s>, therefore the understanding of <s>Lolara</s> as <s>Lavapura</s> (city of <s>Lava</s>) is also appropriate.
	And thus in the eighty-fifth verse of the first <s>taraṅga</s> (chapter) of <s>Paṇḍita</s> <s>Kalhaṇa</s>'s <s>Rājataraṅgiṇī</s>:
By him, having completed a <s>koṭi</s> (ten million) of stone houses devoid of sixteen defects,
the city <s>Lolara</s> was caused to be built. //

It is inferred that this name <s>Lolar</s> arose through corruption of the word <s>Lavapura</s>.
Some translators of the <s>Rājataraṅgiṇī</s> composed in the Persian language [state]:
That king named <s>Lava</s> was always exceedingly fond of song.
Therefore, during his reign, the people who dwelt in the city named <s>Lolar</s> which he had established, fully recognizing the song-loving nature of the contented king, devoted themselves unhesitatingly to the study of singing, and all became skilled in the art of music.
Thus, in the domain of singing in the Kashmiri language, they stood singing the name of that very king, "<s>Lava</s>, <s>Lava</s>," at the very beginning of a song.
With the passage of great time, from that king's name "<s>Lava</s>, <s>Lava</s>," the word "<s>Lolo</s>" became manifest through corruption, and by that very word <s>Lolo</s> that region too became renowned.
Therefore they write in their books that the name of this place is <s>Lolav</s>, and so forth.
Even in the present time, this word "<s>Luḥluḥ</s>" in the Kashmiri language is used in the middle of a song for metrical completion and as a term of address for the beloved being described in the song — this is known to all people.
In this district (<s>puragaṇa</s>), there is also one such village,
whose name all people in the present time call <s>Lulur</s>.
Therefore, by the name of this very village, this entire district also came to be designated by the word <s>Lolav</s> — thus
some villagers and townspeople establish their opinion.
That an entire district can be designated by a single centrally located village is known in other places as well.
For instance, the district called <s>Nāgām</s> is designated by the word <s>Nāgām</s> after just one centrally located village called <s>Kasavanāgām</s>.
The villagers, however, proclaim the name of this region known as <s>Lolar</s> as <s>Lolav Pargaṇa</s>.
Moreover, the name by which this village known as <s>Lulur</s> is called, which the entire district also bears,
they call it <s>Lālpor</s>.
In the coming and going to this <s>Lolar</s> region, there is also a mountain in the middle,
which one must always climb for travel in either direction.
This district lies between two districts called <s>Kramarājya</s> and <s>Utar Khuyahom</s>,
from where travelers can find a route through both of these two districts.
Since this region is situated on the border of <s>Kramarājya</s> as well, it is indeed fitting that in its etymology, its secondary position and other details are also mentioned.
However, <s>Kalhaṇa</s> has written in his book that King <s>Lava</s> built a city by completing eighty-four lakhs of stone houses, [the total] being one crore lacking sixteen lakhs, and so forth.
Those houses have been destroyed in the present time due to the passage of a very long period, and therefore are no longer visible.
But heaps of stones are seen abundantly everywhere, from which it is known that those stones must be the remains and traces of those very houses.
The first village of this <s>Lolav</s> district is renowned by the name <s>Khumariyāl</s>, and the last village is renowned by the name <s>Lālpor</s>.
In the middle of this village of <s>Khumariyāl</s>, there is a reservoir with extremely cold water.
Moreover, near it is the village of <s>Caṇḍī</s>, which has a reservoir that is the abode of the goddess <s>Caṇḍī</s>.
The name of that <s>Caṇḍī</s> village in the local language is <s>Caṇāgom</s>.
Many other such villages similarly serve as abodes of deities — may there be well-being.
